questions.q: What is the fundamental architectural difference between a CPU core and a GPU core?
options: GPU cores run at a higher clock speed, which is the entire source of their advantage
CPU cores are few and complex, optimized for low-latency single-thread work; GPU cores are numerous and simple, optimized for throughput across many threads at once
CPU cores and GPU cores are architecturally identical; the only difference is how many of them are packed onto a chip
GPU cores each handle a completely different instruction stream, while CPU cores all execute the same instruction
questions.explain: A CPU has a handful of sophisticated, latency-optimized cores with deep pipelines and branch prediction. A GPU has thousands of simpler, throughput-optimized cores designed to run the same operation across massive amounts of data in parallel.

questions.q: Why does deep learning map so well onto GPU hardware?
options: Neural network training primarily involves string parsing and branching logic, which GPUs accelerate natively
GPUs include a built-in neural network interpreter that CPUs lack
Deep learning workloads are mostly disk I/O bound, and GPUs have faster storage controllers

The forward and backward passes of a neural network are dominated by matrix multiplications — exactly the independent, repetitive multiply-accumulate operations a GPU's parallel cores are built to execute
questions.explain: Dense layers, convolutions (via im2col), and transformer attention all reduce to matrix multiplication. That's precisely the workload pattern GPU cores, organized for SIMT execution, are designed to accelerate.

questions.q: What does SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads) describe?
options: A GPU execution model where one instruction is issued and executed simultaneously across many threads, each operating on different data
A networking protocol used to transfer data between a CPU and a GPU over PCIe
A compression format used to shrink model weights before inference
A CPU-only feature that has no equivalent concept on GPUs
questions.explain: SIMT groups threads (warps of 32 on NVIDIA GPUs) that all execute the same instruction at once, each on its own data element — the mechanism that lets thousands of simple cores process a matrix multiply's inner loop in parallel.

questions.q: What do Tensor Cores add beyond a GPU's general-purpose CUDA cores?
options: They replace CUDA cores entirely on every modern GPU
They only matter for video decoding, not for AI workloads
They are a marketing label with no distinct hardware behavior from CUDA cores

Specialized circuits that perform a small matrix multiply-accumulate in a single operation, often at reduced precision (FP16/BF16/INT8/FP8), delivering far more throughput per clock on matmul-heavy workloads
questions.explain: Tensor Cores, introduced with the Volta architecture, are purpose-built for the matrix multiply-accumulate pattern that dominates deep learning, and they operate at reduced precision for extra throughput — this is distinct from simply having more general CUDA cores.

questions.q: Why is 'mixed-precision training' standard practice on modern GPUs?
options: It runs the bulk of matmul compute in FP16/BF16 for speed while accumulating results in FP32, balancing throughput against numerical stability
It is required by law for any model trained on cloud infrastructure
It eliminates the need for a GPU and allows training to run entirely on CPU vector extensions
It permanently converts the model's final weights to 8-bit integers regardless of accuracy impact
questions.explain: Mixed precision uses lower-precision formats (FP16/BF16) for most of the matmul-heavy compute to exploit Tensor Core throughput, while keeping FP32 accumulation where needed to avoid numerical instability.
